title: Effectiveness of interventions for improving educational outcomes for people with disabilities in low- and middle-income countries: A systematic review.
principal: the authors of Effectiveness of interventions for improving educational outcomes for people with disabilities in low- and middle-income countries: A systematic review.

objections.claim_quoted: A 2025 Campbell systematic review concludes that a range of individual-level interventions work to improve educational outcomes among people with disabilities in low- and middle-income countries, but that there is little research on systemic or school-level change [1].
objections.objection: The page states 'work' flatly. The authors attach an explicit instruction to read their findings cautiously, and this does not appear next to the claim.
objections.source_says: "However, the findings of this review must be interpreted cautiously, given the low confidence in study methods, severe heterogeneity and significant publication bias." (Discussion/Summary of main results, as it appears in the full-text PDF). The abstract's Main Results also say: "Across studies, heterogeneity is high, and risk of publication bias varies but was frequently high."
objections.locator: Discussion (summary of main results); Abstract, Main Results
objections.why: The page does mention low confidence and bias in later sentences. But the headline claim that interventions 'work' is not tied to the authors' own warning that the findings are inflated by weak design, heterogeneity and publication bias. A reader of the first sentence alone gets a stronger result than the authors claim.

quotation_check.note: the quotation is not in the held text

objections.claim_quoted: Interventions aimed at skills for learning showed significant effects on literacy, cognitive skills, handwriting and numeracy, and the review calls these effects large but based on a low number of studies [1].
objections.objection: The page omits the pooled estimates and their confidence intervals. These show the 'large' effects are very imprecise, and for literacy the lower bound is almost zero. The review also flags potentially high publication bias.
objections.source_says: Literacy d = 2.46 (0.01 to 4.90) k = 4 n = 389 I ² = 93% Egger's test 3.61 ( t = 1.66, p = 0.24) Large effect based on a low number of studies with high heterogeneity and potentially high publication bias
objections.locator: 5.3 Effects of interventions, Table 14 (Effects of interventions), Skills for learning, Literacy row
objections.why: The page says 'significant' and 'large' and notes the low number of studies. It does not say the effects come from k = 2 to 4 studies per outcome with I² of 85–93%, and with intervals running from near zero to implausibly large. The direction is supported, but the size is not.
objections.source_says_first: Table of pooled effects: "Literacy | d = 2.46 (0.01 to 4.90) k = 4 n = 389 I² = 93% ... Large effect based on a low number of studies with high heterogeneity and potentially high publication bias". "Numeracy · d = 4.60 (0.69 to 8.50) k = 2 n = 110 I² = 85% ... High effect based on a low number of studies with high heterogeneity." "Handwriting · d = 4.86 (0.25 to 9.48) k = 2 n = 101".

objections.claim_quoted: The effects on literacy, cognitive skills, handwriting and numeracy were significant, and the review calls all of them large but based on a low number of studies [1].
objections.objection: This repeats the same omission. The review describes these effects differently by outcome and flags high heterogeneity and, for literacy, potentially high publication bias. The page presents them as uniformly 'large'.
objections.source_says: Large effect based on a low number of studies with high heterogeneity and potentially high publication bias
objections.locator: Section 5.3 Effects of interventions, Table 14 (Literacy row; the same wording also appears in the Cognitive skills row)
objections.why: Under the rule against fixing a fault in one place and leaving it in another, this sentence needs the same qualification. 'Large but low number of studies' leaves out the review's separate heterogeneity and publication-bias flags.
objections.source_says_first: "Numeracy ... High effect based on a low number of studies with high heterogeneity." "Handwriting ... Large effect based on a low number of studies with low heterogeneity." "Literacy ... Large effect based on a low number of studies with high heterogeneity and potentially high publication bias." Also: "The publication bias for numeracy and handwriting cannot be assessed due to low sample size."

objections.claim_quoted: According to the source, all but one study received an overall rating of low confidence in study findings [1].
objections.objection: The page gives the low-confidence rating but not the study-design makeup behind it. Only four of the 28 included studies were randomised trials, and that is the evidence for 'works'.
objections.source_says: The four high confidence ratings were given for RCTs.
objections.locator: Results, design ratings for confidence in study findings (paragraph following the list of studies rated low on design)
objections.why: It matters to the 'work' conclusion that 24 of 28 studies were non-randomised designs. The page lists one RCT and one uncontrolled before-and-after study as examples of the range, but never gives the proportion.
objections.source_says_first: "Of the 28 studies included, four were RCTs." (Summary and Results, overview of included studies). The review also says "Generally, methodological details were poorly reported."

objections.claim_quoted: They also recommend a focus on interventions that address attendance, enrolment, completion and transition to higher levels of education, not only individual skills [1].
objections.objection: The page gives the recommendation but not the finding behind it. No included study measured attendance, enrolment or completion. This is the evidence gap that explains the recommendation.
objections.source_says: "No study looked at outcomes related to attendance, enrolment, and completion of people with disabilities in education."
objections.locator: Results – outcome categories table (Attendance, enrolment, and completion); Authors' Conclusions 7.1
objections.why: The review's headline outcomes are access and persistence in school, which are the gaps named in its own background. The page says no studies covered two intervention categories. It does not say that no studies measured the outcomes of attendance, enrolment and completion, so the evidence on 'educational outcomes' is narrower than the page implies. 'Work' applies only to skills and attainment measures and conditions for inclusion.

objections.claim_quoted: The authors call for studies with larger samples, more rigorous designs and standardised measures [1].
objections.objection: The page omits the authors' diagnosis of why Children with disabilities fall behind: school systems are not set up to teach them. This is the premise of the twin-track recommendation.
objections.source_says: "Children with disabilities fall behind in educational outcomes as the current school systems are not set up to teach children with different impairment types."
objections.why: The page reports the twin-track recommendation without the authors' stated reason. The reason supports the point that individual-level interventions alone cannot close the gap. The conclusion stands, but its rationale is missing.
